A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MotionPercept/MotionCritic research, with matching core methods and results. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotator-consensus results, motion-quality metric comparisons and user studies evaluating generator fine-tuning.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds annotator-disjoint evaluation, AMASS experiments, robustness tests and ensemble analyses.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 removes v1's sampled random scalar r and its extra argument to the critic-loss mapping. This is a limited revision to the stated algorithm; the architecture, objectives and principal fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged. Because Equation 4 already omitted r in v1, an implementation change is not established.

E1.justification: v2 retains HumanAct12, UESTC and HumanML3D/FLAME coverage, while adding AMASS ground-truth motions and evaluation under Gaussian corruption, variable sequence lengths and resampling. Appendix B substantially broadens the motion distributions and input conditions tested.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Jerk, PoseNDF, NPSS and NDMS to the retained comparators. Appendix B.6 additionally evaluates logistic-regression, SVM and MLP metric ensembles, while Appendix C.1 compares a DRaFT-LV-style one-step fine-tuning alternative.

E3.justification: v2 adds annotator-disjoint splitting with explicit retraining, a separate ensemble training/test split, controlled perturbation and resampling protocols, and longer fine-tuning comparisons. Generator accuracy and diversity are additionally evaluated. Section 5.1 revises reported training/test pair counts from 46,761/5,829 to 46,740/5,823 without establishing that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's retained per-action and fine-tuning analyses, v2 adds error-confidence analysis, Gaussian-noise sensitivity, sequence-length/interpolation tests, annotator-disjoint robustness, feature-addition/removal ablations, SHAP analysis and alternative fine-tuning schedules. These directly investigate previously untested failure conditions and sources of performance.

E5.justification: The repeated-training statement and per-action error bars are retained unchanged. v2 additionally reports descriptive score variability through mean/std/max/min summaries in Tables 8–9 and the standard-deviation band in Figure 11(B). These describe variation across motions, rather than establishing additional training runs or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 scores remain unchanged, including MotionCritic's 85.07% MDM and 81.43% FLAME accuracy. Substantial new results include 80.13%/79.24% under the annotator-disjoint protocol, AMASS robustness findings and ensemble results. Table 12 reports 85.17% for the MLP versus 84.96% for MotionCritic alone on its separate split; these are not improvements over the original evaluation setting.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, Bradley-Terry objective, diffusion and loss equations, and Elo formulas are retained. New discussion of non-smoothness and relative preferences is empirical or explanatory, with no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The three principal contributions remain MotionPercept, perceptually aligned evaluation and efficient generator fine-tuning. The conclusion adds a limited qualification: the critic should serve as an evaluation metric or fine-tuning loss, but not both simultaneously, and should not be interpreted as a distance measure.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and limitations: it motivates synthetic-only preference collection, discusses low-confidence errors and object-interaction outliers, and explains the optimization difficulties associated with a non-smooth score landscape. It also argues that MotionCritic captures much heuristic information and discusses annotator representativeness and metric-use boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents comparator implementations, 60-frame/24-fps motion generation, AMASS preprocessing, ensemble architecture and independent user-study participants. Conversely, it removes v1's dataset datasheet, including explicit licensing, collection dates, maintenance/contact information and raw-data availability details. The shared project link remains.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning relative to HuTuMotion, improved motion-distance metrics, DRaFT and MotionRL, alongside additional perceptual background citations. The datasheet reference disappears with that appendix. These extend the literature discussion while retaining the central positioning relative to MoBERT and reward-based fine-tuning.

P1.justification: Most existing main-text prose and section order are retained. v2 expands the fine-tuning explanation, locally rewrites related work, updates affiliations and citation style, and reorganizes appendix subsections after removing the datasheet and contents page. This is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material, including Figures 10–14 and Tables 7–15, expands the old fine-tuning figure with a third panel, and enlarges Table 1. New Table 2 partly tabulates previously plotted metrics while adding accuracy and diversity. Retained displays are relocated within the ICLR layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central metric's validation through annotator-disjoint retraining, broader comparators and AMASS robustness, failure and ablation analyses. These address important gaps in v1's evidence about generalization and reliability, while clearer usage limits improve interpretation. Removing the datasheet and overstating Table 2's accuracy improvement are drawbacks: accuracy at step 600 remains 0.98 and later declines. Nevertheless, the central validation gains outweigh these losses.
